Perform hierarchical clustering for heatmap

Source: R/heat_map_clust.R
heat_map_clust.Rd

Perform hierarchical clustering for heatmap

Usage

heat_map_clust(
  x,
  tree = "row",
  dist = "euclidean",
  method = "complete",
  scale = FALSE,
  cut = NULL,
  order = "default",
  max = 5000,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

matrix-like object to cluster - its numeric columns. Distances and linkage are computed in compiled code (with dist and hclust for the methods it doesn't cover). With a supplied hclust object and order, the rows of x (or its columns when they don't match) are the leaves of the tree.

tree

indicates whether hierarchical clustering should be performed by "row" or "column". Optionally a custom object of class "dist" (clustered using method) or "hclust" which will be updated with cluster labels as specified by cut. Any clusters already stored in a supplied hclust object are replaced when cut is supplied.

dist

method passed to dist to compute distance matrix, set to "euclidean" by default. Also supports "cosine" for cosine distance (1 - cosine similarity), "pearson", "spearman" or "kendall" for one minus the correlation (rows without variation are treated as uncorrelated), or a function that takes the matrix being clustered (one row per leaf) and returns a dist object or a square matrix of distances. Names ignore case and can be abbreviated (e.g. "pear").

method

agglomeration method, one of the methods of hclust ("ward.D", "ward.D2", "single", "complete", "average", "mcquitty", "median" or "centroid", which can be abbreviated), set to "complete" by default.

scale

logical indicating whether branch heights should be scaled for better visualisation, set to FALSE by default.

cut

value from 0 to less than 1 specifying the tree cutpoint as a proportion of the tree height (for non-cosine distances) or as an absolute cosine distance threshold (when dist = "cosine"), or a value greater than or equal to 1 indicating the number of desired clusters.

order

how the branches of the dendrogram are ordered: "default" keeps the order from hclust, "olo" flips branches to minimise the distances between neighbouring leaves (optimal leaf ordering) and "mean" orders branches by their mean values (heatmap orders them by the sum of their leaves' means instead, which favours small branches). Optimal leaf ordering is exact for up to 2000 leaves, which takes about a second; its time grows with the cube of the number of leaves, so larger trees are ordered in blocks (of 2000 leaves, down to 100 for the largest trees), each ordered exactly, with the blocks then ordered and turned to meet their neighbours. 200,000 leaves take about 3 seconds.

max

the largest number of rows (or columns) clustered exactly, set to 5000 by default. Exact clustering needs the distances between every pair of rows, so its memory and time grow with the square of their number. Larger data is clustered in two stages: a sample of max rows (drawn with a fixed seed, so the result is the same each time) is clustered exactly and its dendrogram split into groups of about 200 rows of the data, every row joins the group of its nearest group medoid, and each group is clustered exactly beneath the sample's dendrogram. The dendrogram then shows the structure of the whole data down to the groups, and within each group: 100,000 rows take about 2 seconds. Set to Inf to always cluster exactly.

...

additional arguments passed to dist (e.g. p) or hclust (members); others are ignored with a warning.

Value

object of class hclust which describes the tree produced by the clustering process. Branch heights are rescaled to the range [0, 1] for display. When cut is supplied, the returned object also contains a cut element holding the cluster assigned to each leaf in dendrogram order. A tree clustered in two stages (more than max rows) has a two_stage element giving the size of the sample and the number of groups.

Details

Single, complete, average, McQuitty and Ward linkage are computed by the nearest-neighbour chain algorithm, which builds the same tree as hclust when the distances are distinct. When distances are tied (common for integer, binary or rounded data), more than one tree is correct and the two can choose differently between tied merges, so the tree - and the branches above the tied merges - can differ from the one hclust returns while being equally valid. Centroid and median linkage use hclust itself. Missing and infinite values are left out of the distances between rows (as dist leaves out missing values); rows that share no values can't be clustered.

Author

Dillon Hammill (dillon.hammill21@gmail.com)

Examples

# Hierarchical clustering
heat_map_hclust <- heat_map_clust(mtcars, cut = 5)
